candidates.title: Optimal-transport flow matching for stochastic model ipdating
candidates.abstract: Deep generative models have attracted considerable attention as inference engines for stochastic model updating. Among these deep generative models, conditional flow matching offers a particularly efficient formulation, in which a continuous transport map from a latent distribution to the posterior is learned by regression against optimal-transport probability paths, avoiding both the invertibility constraints of normalising flows and the iterative denoising of diffusion models. However, its performance in engineering model updating has not been examined against an established baseline such as the Bayesian updating framework under controlled conditions. In this work, conditional flow matching is therefore assessed against the Bayesian model updating approach with transitional Markov chain Monte Carlo, in which the Bhattacharyya distance provides the approximate likelihood for the Bayesian approach. The two methods are assessed with respect to posterior fidelity, evaluated by statistical distances against the known ground truth and computational expenditure in model evaluations, with the offline training budget reported separately from the inference cost of each subsequent conditioning. A 3-DOF spring–mass system with uncertain stiffness parameters serves as the benchmark. Since the calibrated posterior constitutes the input description upon which subsequent reliability assessment depends, the accuracy and the marginal cost of the updating step both bear directly on reliability computations. In addition, the amortised nature of the learned transport map is discussed in this work, as it permits the posterior to be re-evaluated under new observations at negligible cost, which is a property of practical relevance to reliability assessment under sequentially acquired monitoring data.

candidates.title: Latent Style-Based Quantum Wasserstein GAN for Drug Design
candidates.abstract: Abstract The development of new drugs is a tedious, time-consuming, and expensive process for which the average costs are estimated to be up to around $2.5 billion. The first step in this long process is the design of the new drug, for which de novo drug design, assisted by artificial intelligence, has blossomed in recent years and has revolutionized the field. In particular, generative artificial intelligence has delivered promising results in drug discovery and development, reducing costs and time to solution. However, classical generative models, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), can be difficult to train and are prone to mode collapse. Quantum computing may be an avenue to overcome some of these issues, providing compact models with far fewer trainable parameters and thereby enhancing the generalizability of GANs. We propose a new latent style-based quantum Wasserstein GAN (QGAN) for drug design, combining a variational autoencoder that maps molecular structures into a latent space with a hybrid quantum GAN. Our pipeline is benchmarked against the classical models of the industry-relevant MOSES suite. Style-based noise reuploading at every rotational gate and a Wasserstein gradient penalty are used to improve trainability and to mitigate mode collapse. Training and large-scale sampling with circuits of up to 15 qubits are performed on noiseless quantum simulators to validate our architecture. We present an inference-only demonstration on a 156-qubit IBM Heron quantum computer using a five-qubit setup, sampling 2,500 new molecules, to investigate the effect of quantum noise. Our default QGAN, using 110 trainable generator parameters, reaches statistically comparable overall performance and statistically significant gains on selected drug-relevant metrics relative to both the MOSES classical latent GAN baseline, which contains about 700,000 trainable parameters for the generator, and a classical latent GAN with matched generator capacity.

candidates.title: The ternary complex structure as a foundation for structure-guided molecular glue design
candidates.abstract: Molecular glues are opening up new therapeutic areas by turning previously undruggable and intractable proteins into tractable targets through the formation or stabilisation of a ternary complex between two proteins. The present review focuses on how such structures are obtained and leveraged to guide rational design. Ternary complexes can be classified by protein-protein interface architecture and degree of topological constraint, informing the design process towards a given biological outcome. As with conventional small-molecule drug discovery, structural information provides invaluable insights for rational optimisation of glues, but solving a ternary complex structure remains a significant challenge owing to the underlying three-body equilibrium. Biophysical characterisation of cooperativity and ternary complex half-life not only provides optimisation parameters but also provides a means for prioritising the most promising glues for ternary structural studies by X-ray crystallography or cryogenic electron microscopy. Once solved, a ternary structure enables conventional structure-based design, such as scaffold hopping and surface decoration, and increasingly informs computational methods, though these remain most powerful when grounded in experimental validation. Ternary complex structures for canonical glue systems are now available in relative abundance, providing a foundation for both empirical and computational design; expanding this coverage beyond well-studied glue receptors and binding partners will test how broadly these principles generalise.

candidates.title: A hierarchical evolutionary deep reinforcement learning algorithm for influence maximization in multilayer hypergraphs
candidates.abstract: Multilayer hypergraphs provide a unified representation of influence diffusion in complex networks by coupling relation layers through shared entities and encoding higher-order group interactions as hyperedges. Existing influence maximization (IM) methods have been extensively studied on ordinary graphs and single-layer hypergraphs, yet they leave two structural limitations unresolved. Single-layer methods cannot represent the propagation of an entity across multiple relation semantics, whereas most multilayer methods still use pairwise edges as their basic diffusion units and therefore omit hyperedge-induced group interactions. We address seed selection under the joint effects of multilayer coupling and higher-order influence by introducing Multi-Layer Hypergraph Linear Threshold with Cross-layer Thresholding (MLH-LT-CT). The model combines a dual-threshold intralayer mechanism for hyperedges and nodes with a δ -threshold rule that couples entity states across relation layers. We extend the non-submodularity result for the single-layer hypergraph linear threshold (LT) model to the multilayer setting and show that cross-layer thresholding can further modify the marginal-gain structure induced by intralayer higher-order coordination. Consequently, the classical ( 1 − 1 / e ) guarantee for submodular greedy maximization does not directly apply. To optimize this non-submodular objective, we propose Hierarchical Influence Via Evolution (HIVE), which integrates population-level global search by differential evolution, adaptive seed-selection guidance from a deep Q-network, and topology-guided local refinement. We also establish an incremental-propagation equivalence theorem from the extensivity, idempotence, and monotonicity of the propagation closure. The theorem establishes equality of the final diffusion state obtained by incremental updates and full recomputation; it is not itself a running-time guarantee. Across 11 synthetic and real multilayer hypergraph datasets, HIVE strictly outperformed MA-IM on eight datasets. The ablation and sensitivity analyses further assess the contributions of evolutionary search, reinforcement-learning guidance, and topology-guided refinement; additional threshold scans characterize the transition between saturated, discriminative, and propagation-suppressed regimes; the correctness of incremental state reuse is established theoretically. These results support explicit cross-layer threshold modeling and hierarchical optimization as a coherent approach to non-submodular influence maximization in multilayer higher-order diffusion systems.

candidates.title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design.
candidates.abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

candidates.title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
candidates.abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).

candidates.title: Large-scale prospective evaluation of co-folding across hundreds of Mac1–ligand complexes and three virtual screens
candidates.abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of ligand-bound protein complexes and ranking them by affinity are central problems in drug discovery. While deep learning co-folding methods can help address these challenges, their evaluation has been hampered by the difficulties in assessing independence from training data and insufficiently large test sets. Here we test the ability of co-folding methods to predict the structures of 551 ligands, 489 of which are of sufficient quality for evaluation, bound to the SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 macrodomain (Mac1) that were determined after the training cut-off dates. AlphaFold3 (AF3), Boltz-2, and Chai-1 each reproduced >50% of the Mac1 ligand poses to better than 2 Å RMSD of experiment. Despite the potential for co-folding to describe protein conformational changes that stabilize ligand binding, we did not find that common conformational rearrangements, including peptide flip and a large loop opening, were recapitulated by the co-folding prediction. For AF3 and Chai-1, ligand pose prediction confidence weakly, but significantly, tracked experimental potency, while DOCK3.7 energies were only weakly correlated. Boltz-2 affinity predictions showed the strongest correlation with measured potency and, after calibration, achieved lower mean absolute error than a baseline predictor. We next assessed whether co-folding scores could rescore docking hit-lists to distinguish true ligands from non-binders among hundreds of molecules prospectively experimentally tested against AmpC β-lactamase, the dopamine D4 and the σ 2 receptors. AF3 ligand pose confidence values did not separate true ligands from high-scoring false-positives as effectively as docking scores or Boltz-2 affinity predictions did. Taken together, the modest, but independent correlations of docking score and co-folding confidence or affinity suggests that integrating physics-based and deep-learning and approaches may help with hit prioritization and subsequent optimization in structure-based ligand discovery.

candidates.title: Block-fitness modeling of the global air mobility network
candidates.abstract: Abstract Accurate representations of origin-destination (OD) passenger flows on the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, OD data are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model that treats air mobility as a stochastic process within a sparse maximum-entropy framework, informed by aggregate traffic volumes of individual locations and geographic regions. The model accurately reconstructs both network structure and mobility flows, yielding epidemic spreading trajectories that closely match those obtained using real mobility data. Furthermore, the method can be effectively implemented using open data on flight routes and airport traffic, reducing dependence on proprietary datasets. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for scenario analysis and policy design in global mobility systems.

candidates.title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
candidates.abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

candidates.title: Sampled-Based Guided Quantum Walk: Non-variational quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization
candidates.abstract: We introduce SamBa-GQW, a novel quantum algorithm for solving binary combinatorial optimization problems of arbitrary degree with no use of any classical optimizer. The algorithm is based on a continuous-time quantum walk on the solution space represented as a graph. The walker explores the solution space to find its way to vertices that minimize the cost function of the optimization problem. The key novelty of our algorithm is an offline classical sampling protocol that gives information about the spectrum of the problem Hamiltonian. Then, the extracted information is used to guide the walker to high quality solutions via a quantum walk with a time-dependent hopping rate. We investigate the performance of SamBa-GQW on several quadratic problems, namely MaxCut, maximum independent set, portfolio optimization, and higher-order polynomial problems such as LABS, MAX- k -SAT and a quartic reformulation of the travelling salesperson problem. We empirically demonstrate that SamBa-GQW finds high quality approximate solutions on problems up to a size of n = 30 qubits by only sampling poly( n ) states among 2 n possible decisions. Furthermore, SamBa-GQW compares in par with classically optimized variational approaches, such as the variational guided quantum walk and QAOA (the latter when run on deep circuits). This places Samba-GQW as a promising heuristic to tackle combinatorial problems beyond the NISQ regime.

candidates.title: Adiabatic dressing of quantum enhanced Markov chains
candidates.abstract: Quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo, a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm in which configurations are proposed by a quantum proposer and accepted or rejected by a classical algorithm, has been introduced as a possible method for robust quantum speedup. Previous work has identified competing factors that limit the algorithm's performance: the quantum dynamics should delocalize the system across a range of classical states to propose configurations beyond the reach of simple classical updates, whereas excessive delocalization produces configurations unlikely to be accepted, slowing the chain's convergence. Here, we show that controlling the degree of delocalization by adiabatically dressing the quench protocol can significantly enhance the Markov gap in paradigmatic spin-glass models.

candidates.title: Self-calibrating multi-fidelity active learning for microstrip patch optimization across substrates and bands
candidates.abstract: Physics-aware active learning can reduce the full-wave electromagnetic (EM) cost of microstrip-patch design, but its sampling priors are commonly tuned to one substrate and band. We present an integrated self-calibrating, matching-first, physics-aware active-learning workflow for probe-fed rectangular patches, together with coarse-mesh screening and full-resolution confirmation. The online calibration estimates sampling bands from each run’s observations instead of prescribing case-specific probe locations. Under an equal budget of 37 openEMS simulations, 4 optimizers were compared on 4 substrate/frequency cases using 10 replicate seeds per case. The integrated workflow produced the lowest mean and median final objective in every case, returned a matched design in all forty runs, and was lower than the three baselines in nine of twelve exact directional Mann–Whitney comparisons after within-case Holm adjustment; six contrasts remained significant in a two-sided unpaired analysis and seven in a paired-by-seed sensitivity analysis. Multi-fidelity screening reduced mean equivalent-high-fidelity cost by 19%–46% across cases (36.9% overall) and returned a matched full-resolution design in 39 of 40 runs, although endpoint objective quality was not uniformly preserved. Nominal near-to-far-field calculations for four selected designs gave broadside directivities of 6.51–7.00 dBi and realized gains of 3.59–5.77 dBi. All 12 finer-mesh, larger-domain, and perfectly matched layer (PML) stability checks remained matched; maximum absolute directivity and realized-gain changes were 0.180 and 0.121 dB. A ten-variable E-shaped-patch case study matched all ten integrated-workflow runs. Its advantage over random search was robust to unpaired and paired-by-seed analyses; inference against unstructured radial-basis-function (RBF) surrogate search depended on the treatment of seed blocks, and the genetic comparison remained unresolved. A five-seed in-loop impedance–gain pilot produced a directionally favorable but non-significant hypervolume trend. The evidence is numerical and openEMS-based; no commercial-solver or fabricated prototype validation is claimed.

candidates.title: Collaborative Planning for UAV-UGV Teams under Operational Constraints via Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion
candidates.abstract: Collaborative planning under operational constraints is essential for heterogeneous robot teams in large-scale missions. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) provide rapid area coverage but are limited by onboard energy, while Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) can serve as mobile recharging stations yet are constrained by road-network traversability. Effective collaboration must enforce operational constraints during execution while enabling parallel, coordinated actions. Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have shown promise through token unmasking but have two key limitations: entropy-guided scheduling assumes distributional alignment and reliance on differentiable constraints for diffusion-time optimization. We propose Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion (MEND), which formulates collaborative planning as a conditional masked generative process to generate context-aware action sequences for UAV-UGV teams. MEND introduces a neuro-symbolic diffusion paradigm that constrains conditional masked diffusion policies at execution by reweighting the learned action distribution with a logic-induced admissibility indicator, thereby enforcing compliance with operational constraints. MEND introduces an error-bounded inference scheduling at execution that constructs the unmasking schedule by selecting positions with minimal predictive entropy over the constraint-aware action distribution, enhancing collaborative planning optimality under operational constraints. Extensive experimental results in simulation, on real-world maps, and with physical robot teams demonstrate that MEND advances UAV-UGV collaborative planning under operational constraints.

candidates.title: Parsing altered brain connectivity in neurodevelopmental disorders by integrating graph-based normative modeling and deep generative networks
candidates.abstract: Divergent brain connectivity is thought to underlie the behavioral and cognitive symptoms observed in many neurodevelopmental disorders. Quantifying divergence from neurotypical connectivity patterns offers a promising pathway to inform diagnosis and therapeutic interventions. While advanced neuroimaging techniques, such as diffusion MRI (dMRI), have facilitated the mapping of brain's structural connectome, the challenge lies in accurately modeling developmental trajectories within these complex networked structures to create robust neurodivergence markers. In this work, we present the Brain Representation via Individualized Deep Generative Embedding (BRIDGE) framework, which integrates normative modeling with a bio-inspired deep generative model to create a reference trajectory of connectivity transformation as part of neurotypical development. This will enable the assessment of neurodivergence by comparing individuals to the established neurotypical trajectory. BRIDGE provides a global neurodivergence score based on the difference between connectivity-based brain age and chronological age, along with region-wise neurodivergence maps that highlight localized connectivity differences. Application of BRIDGE to a large cohort of children with autism spectrum disorder demonstrates that the global neurodivergence score correlates with clinical assessments in autism, and the regional map offers insights into the heterogeneity at the individual level in neurodevelopmental disorders. Together, the neurodivergence score and map form powerful tools for quantifying developmental divergence in connectivity patterns, advancing the development of imaging markers for personalized diagnosis and intervention in various clinical contexts.

candidates.title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
candidates.abstract: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(φ^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.

candidates.title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
candidates.abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.

candidates.title: Flow-WLS: Regularized Multistep Integration for Fast Sampling in Generative Flow Matching Models
candidates.abstract: Numerical integration of the probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE) in diffusion and Flow Matching models is fundamentally constrained by a trade-off: low-order solvers (orders 1–2) require substantial step budgets (30+ NFEs) to avoid oversmoothing, while classical explicit high-order multistep schemes (orders 4+) suffer from Adams-Bashforth instability, Runge's phenomenon, and severe noise amplification. In this work, we analyze the breakdown mechanism of high-order polynomial extrapolation in Flow Matching architectures (such as DiT / Cosmos) and introduce Flow-WLS (Weighted Least Squares / Savitzky-Golay Multistep). Instead of fitting an oscillating interpolating polynomial of degree (L-1) through past velocity evaluations, Flow-WLS constrains the trajectory approximation to a regularized low-degree parabola (d=2) fitted over extended history buffers (L=3 to 8 steps) via weighted least squares with exponential memory decay. This inverts the classic curse of multistep solvers: increasing memory depth suppresses discretization noise rather than amplifying it. Empirical evaluations on text-to-image Flow Matching models demonstrate strictly monotonic metric improvements as history expands from L=3 to L=8, achieving an SSIM of 0.8003 at only 10 NFEs (~11 seconds on a consumer GPU) with zero anatomical distortion.

candidates.title: Dog-Breed Text-to-image Flow Matching from Pretraining to Fine-Tuning on 4 Consumer GPUs
candidates.abstract: We generally perceive that training text-to-image diffusion models requires heavy compute: it is true if we aim at a comprehensive frontier model. This understanding prevents people from training their own models when getting started in the field. We develop MiniDog, a framework that enables pretraining diffusion transformers in 55 minutes and fine-tuning in another 15 minutes on four 3090 GPUs. For data, we use 26k dog images from ImageNet and caption them for pretraining and use 2k images generated by FLUX.1-schnell for fine-tuning. We precompute the image and text features and cache them for efficiency. For architecture, we use E2E-INVAE for its semantic latent space, a small transformer with 22M parameters, a small Qwen model for text encoding, and in-context conditioning. For training, we use iREPA and an EUPE perception encoder for acceleration. For evaluation, our repository supports FID, HPSv2 score, PickScore, and various VAE reconstruction metrics.

candidates.title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
candidates.abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

candidates.title: Physics-Informed Multi-Parameter Optimization of Oxide-Based Memristor Characteristics Using Genetic Algorithms
candidates.abstract: Abstract We present a multiobjective, physics-informed optimization framework for oxide-based memristive devices that jointly minimizes forming voltage (Vf) and maximizes memory contrast (HRS/LRS). The proposed approach integrates COMSOL Multiphysics with MATLAB through a genetic algorithm (GA), enabling self-consistent electrothermal simulations and systematic exploration of a high-dimensional design space encompassing geometrical, electrical, thermal, and operational parameters. By optimizing 13 key variables, the GA efficiently identifies optimal trade-offs between switching efficiency and resistance ratio. The optimization results demonstrate a substantial enhancement in device performance, with the high-resistance-state to low-resistance-state ratio (HRS/LRS) improved by up to 21× relative to the reference device, while alternative optimized configurations achieve a reduction in Vf down to 0.7× of the reference value. A parameter-importance analysis based on a random forest model highlights oxide thickness and effective electrical and thermal conductivities as influential parameters. Importantly, the optimization further reveals nontrivial multiparameter trade-offs, demonstrating that reductions in Vf and enhancements in HRS/LRS can be simultaneously achieved through coordinated tuning of geometrical, material, and pulse-related parameters beyond simple intuitive design rules. Overall, the MATLAB–COMSOL co-optimization strategy provides a scalable and generalizable computational design methodology for next-generation low-power, high-contrast RRAM devices, and offers quantitative insights into the coupled physical mechanisms underlying filament formation and rupture.

candidates.title: Molecular Conformation as a Determinant of Self-Assembly in Sequence-Isomeric Tripeptides
candidates.abstract: Abstract In this work, we evaluate whether computed conformational ensembles of seven tripeptides─the six C-terminal amidated D/Y/F sequence isomers and the closely related sequence FFD─are informative of their self-assembly propensity. Using all-atom molecular dynamics (AA-MD) simulations and intramolecular side-chain dihedral angles as a collective variable, we calculate conformational free-energy landscapes (FELs) for these sequences. We then introduce a novel method to numerically characterize the computed FELs and find a correlation between thermal conformational accessibility and a sequence’s tendency to self-assemble or remain in solution. In addition, we evaluate and rationalize the impact of water model selection on conformational ensembles in terms of peptide-water interaction strengths, and also investigate the influence of ionization state on conformation. The presented methodology implicitly accounts for amino acid sequence context, which is a major determinant of divergent properties for sequence isomers. It also has a low associated computational cost, making use of single-molecule simulations to predict supramolecular assembly outcomes. These features are an important advancement toward a general scheme for the theory-informed design of peptide materials.

candidates.title: Sequence-based artificial intelligence-guided inhibitory peptides to counteract AAV neutralizing antibodies in gene therapy.
candidates.abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have demonstrated strong clinical efficacy across multiple monogenic disorders, yet neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) remain major barriers to vector redosing and durable transduction. To address this limitation, we developed a sequence-based artificial intelligence framework integrating Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and Evolutionary Scale Modeling with Low-Rank Adaptation (ESM-LoRA) to identify human-tolerant, virus-specific motifs across human and viral proteins using sliding-window analyses and multi-layer fine-tuning. Using capsid-derived segments from AAV2 and AAV843, we prioritized surface-accessible, virus-polarized peptides as candidate decoys and evaluated their ability to block AAV-targeted antibodies. The models achieved high accuracy in distinguishing human versus viral fragments, and selected peptides bound AAV-specific antibodies with nanomolar affinity, competitively restored capsid binding, and recovered >60% of baseline transduction in the presence of NAbs. In mouse models with pre-existing or redosing-induced antibodies, coadministration of decoy peptides and an IgG-degrading enzyme reduced high-titer NAbs to approximately 1:4 and restored hepatic transgene expression without detectable inflammatory or peptide-specific immune responses. A contrastive variational autoencoder (VAE) further generated non-natural peptides with broader epitope coverage. These results support sequence-driven AI design of short, low-immunogenicity decoy peptides as a translational strategy to mitigate NAb interference and enhance the feasibility of AAV redosing.

candidates.title: Fast Solution Methods for the Classical 0–1 Knapsack Problem
candidates.abstract: The classical 0--1 knapsack problem is among the simplest integer programs to state and among the most instructive problems for understanding why algorithm selection must follow instance structure. An input contains items with positive integer weights and profits, and the task is to choose a maximum-profit subset whose total weight does not exceed a capacity. The problem is weakly NP-hard, yet many large instances are solved quickly because exact algorithms exploit moderate numeric parameters, strong linear relaxations, dominance relations, or a small set of uncertain variables near the fractional break item. This review develops a theory-guided account of the principal fast solution methods for the classical problem. It proves the correctness and complexity of weight-indexed and profit-indexed dynamic programming, explains sparse Pareto-frontier implementations and reconstruction, derives the fractional-knapsack upper bound used by branch-and-bound methods, and establishes the correctness of meet-in-the-middle search. It then presents the core concept that underlies influential practical solvers and gives a detailed proof of the standard profit-scaling fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. Modern advances based on structured min-plus convolution are placed within this classical landscape rather than treated as isolated results. The central conclusion is that there is no universally fastest knapsack algorithm. Small item counts favor meet-in-the-middle search, moderate capacities or total profits favor dynamic programming, favorable density structure favors core-based exact methods, and very large numeric coefficients favor approximation. A final decision framework translates these theoretical distinctions into an implementable solver-selection policy while identifying open questions concerning adaptivity, certified switching among methods, memory efficiency, and realistic hard-instance generation.

candidates.title: The rise of agentic AI in drug discovery from static tools to autonomous virtual scientists
candidates.abstract: Driven by large language models, AI agents are transforming drug discovery, enabling AI to break free from task-specific tools and advance toward the vision of autonomous virtual scientists. This perspective reviews applications across the R&D lifecycle. To evaluate system maturity, we introduce a 6-level "Spectrum of Agentic Autonomy." We advocate for novel evaluation paradigms centered on full-chain traceability and outline adoption barriers, positioning AI agents as pragmatic scientist-in-the-loop co-pilots.

candidates.title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.

candidates.title: Network Pharmacology in Drug Discovery: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Directions Toward Precision Medicine
candidates.abstract: Network pharmacology (NP) is an innovative drug discovery method that provides a comprehensive view of drug-body interactions through complex biological networks. Each drug modulates specific network nodes, and understanding these interactions helps predict therapeutic effects and side effects. By integrating diverse data types and advanced computational methods, NP enables more accurate identification of new drug targets, accelerating the development of effective, targeted therapies. It also supports personalized medicine by tailoring treatments to individual biological profiles. This review examines the fundamentals and strategic significance of NP in drug discovery. Network-based approaches unravel complex molecular interactions and discover drug targets with high accuracy. Holistic NP implementation integrates omics datasets and computational tools to deliver actionable insights. The difficulty of screening all drug pairs due to time and cost constraints has driven the development of computational methods to predict side effects efficiently. NP holds transformative potential for precision medicine, promising improved patient outcomes and innovative treatments across many diseases. Conclusively, NP is transforming drug discovery by providing a whole-view approach to drug interactions and enabling effective, personalized therapeutic interventions.

candidates.title: MtbAIM: AI/ML-guided endpoint-specific prediction of small-molecule activity across drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
candidates.abstract: The emergence of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) presents a major challenge to drug discovery, as compounds active against drug-susceptible (DS) isolates may not retain comparable inhibitory activity against drug-resistant (DR) isolates. Here, we developed an AI/ML workflow to independently prioritize small molecules separately against DS and DR isolates of M.tb and predict MIC, MIC90, and MIC99 as distinct quantitative endpoints. Following curation of data retrieved from the ChEMBL repository, molecular-activity datasets comprised 25,645 and 3,749 compounds tested against whole cell DS and DR isolates respectively. Molecular representations were generated using RDKit descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, along with embeddings from ChemBERTa, MolCLR, and Uni-Mol, and evaluated for binary activity classification and endpoint-specific regression. The best-performing DS classifier combined RDKit/Morgan features with ExtraTrees (balanced accuracy 0.782; AUROC 0.864; AUPRC 0.870), while histogram gradient boosting using the same features performed best for DR classification (balanced accuracy 0.762; AUROC 0.836; AUPRC 0.880). Similarly, RDKit/Morgan features combined with tree-based regressors achieved the best overall performance across all six DS/DR regression endpoints, with pooled out-of-fold RMSE values ranging from 0.604 to 0.784 pMIC units. To facilitate broader application, we developed MtbAIM (https://github.com/jasdeep002/MtbAIM), a Google Colab-based prediction platform that enables users to assess and prioritize small molecules against DS and DR isolates of M.tb.

candidates.title: A History-Response-Conditioned FiLM-CNN and Transfer Learning–Based Approach for Pressure Transient Analysis of Multiphase Fractured Horizontal Wells
candidates.abstract: Abstract Pressure-transient responses of fractured horizontal wells under multiphase-flow conditions are jointly affected by phase behavior, relative permeability, saturation distribution, and fracture conductivity, resulting in complex pressure and pressure-derivative signatures. Conventional numerical simulation is computationally expensive, whereas direct deep-learning training is constrained by the limited availability of multiphase samples. To address these challenges, a history-response-conditioned FiLM-CNN combined with transfer learning is proposed for multiphase pressure-transient analysis. Based on parameter combinations generated using Sobol sequence sampling, a semi-analytical model is employed to construct a large-scale single-phase database, and a commercial numerical simulator is used to generate approximately 800 oil–gas two-phase samples. Early-time pressure responses and key static parameters are jointly encoded as conditioning information and injected into the CNN through feature-wise linear modulation, enabling the network to adaptively adjust its intermediate features according to different reservoir conditions and fracture parameters. A dual-task learning objective with a pressure–pressure-derivative consistency constraint is introduced to improve prediction performance. In the multiphase prediction stage, static-input reconfiguration, pretrained-weight inheritance, and a freeze–unfreeze fine-tuning strategy are adopted to transfer the pretrained single-phase model to the multiphase prediction task. The results show that the proposed model achieves a pressure-prediction R2 of 0.9996 on the single-phase test set. Dual-task learning reduces the MAPE of the pressure derivative by 77.96%, while transfer learning reduces the pressure and pressure-derivative prediction errors for most multiphase test samples compared with training from scratch. The proposed framework improves multiphase prediction capability under limited-sample conditions and provides an efficient and stable surrogate model for pressure-transient analysis of fractured horizontal wells.

candidates.title: Deciphering isonicotinylation and mast cell-associated pathogenic patterns in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: evidence from ensemble learning-driven multi-omics and in vitro validation
candidates.abstract: Background Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is dystrophin-deficiency skeletal and cardiac muscle disease. Protein post-translational modification (PTM) and aberrant immune cell activation play a key role in its pathogenesis. Objective Our study aims to investigate isonicotinylation (Kinic)-associated signature modulatory patterns in mast cells and DMD pathogenesis. Methods We first performed integrated bioinformatic methods, such as WGCNA, GSVA, and CIBERSORT to identify Kinic and mast cell (KM)-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in DMD patient muscle bulk profiles (GSE38417 and GSE109178). Next, consensus clustering and assembling machine learning pipeline identified KM-associated diagnostic model and molecular subgroups in training the DMD patient muscle bulk set (GSE6011), and then, diagnostic model performance was examined in the independent DMD patient muscle bulk set (GSE32720). In addition, SHAP analysis decoded the main contributor in KM-associated diagnostic model construction, and contributor molecular and immune characters in DMD were estimated in GSE6011 and the DMD mouse muscle single-cell transcriptomic dataset (GSE213925) assisted by computational virtual cells. In addition, the deep learning framework and network pharmacology identified the drug synergy strategy for the treatment of DMD. Finally, the in vitro assay identified expression patterns of the main contributor. Results KM-associated molecular patterns can potentially guide the diagnostic and molecular stratification for DMD patients. USP18 can be considered an upregulated and mast cell-distributed hub gene involved in pathogenesis of DMD. In addition, finafloxacin with BRD-K10482608 can be considered two potential therapeutic candidates for DMD patient clinical applications. Conclusion Our investigation described a novel forecasting and therapeutic model for DMD patients, which potentially enhances DMD patient clinical translation.

candidates.title: Bayesian Ambiguity-Contraction-Based Adaptive Robust Markov Decision Processes for Adversarial Surveillance Missions
candidates.abstract: Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCAs) are envisioned to enable autonomous intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions in contested environments, where adversaries may act strategically to deceive or evade detection. These missions pose challenges due to model uncertainty and the need for safe, real-time decision-making. Robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) provide worst-case guarantees but are limited by static ambiguity sets that capture initial uncertainty without adapting to new observations. This paper presents an adaptive RMDP framework tailored to ISR missions with CCAs. We introduce a mission-specific formulation in which the CCA alternates between movement and sensing states. Adversarial uncertainty is represented by finite threat prototypes defining observation, exposure, and state–action transition models. Our approach incrementally refines policies by eliminating inconsistent threat models, allowing the CCA to move from worst-case protection toward more efficient mission policies while maintaining robustness. We establish fixed-point stability, agreement with nominal planning as credible sets identify the true node-specific threat prototypes, and a conservative expected value guarantee while those prototypes remain credible. Experiments under Gaussian and non-Gaussian threat models across diverse network topologies show higher mission rewards and fewer exposure events compared to nominal and static robust planners.
